prompt.context: Your client, Dr. Rossman, has invented an amazing product; he has discovered the chemical formula for Magic Eye Drops. One drop in each eye will cure short or long-sightedness in any patient. However, Dr. Rossman is a scientist, not a businessman, and has come to our firm because he wants to sell the rights to his Magic Eye Drops to a business that will commercialize the invention.
prompt.question: What should his asking price be?

clarifying_info.q: Does Dr. Rossman have patent protection?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. He has secured an exclusive, worldwide patent for the next 20 years. After the patent expires, generic versions will quickly be developed.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any known side effects or risks?
clarifying_info.a: No known side effects or risks.

clarifying_info.q: Which market should we focus on?
What discount rate should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the discount rate is zero.
For this case, focus on corrective lenses (glasses and contacts) as competitors. Laser surgery is the closest competitor but set it aside for now.

framework: Revenue: estimate via market size × price × patent life
Revenue – Market Size: segment US population by age, apply rate of sight problems and rate of adoption per segment
Revenue – Pricing: choose pricing strategy (cost-based, competitive, or value-based); use corrective lenses as the competitive benchmark (~$200/year)
Revenue – Channels: direct sales, hospitals, eye care providers, pharmacies, corrective lens manufacturers
Competition: laser therapy (closest), contact lenses, glasses
Costs – Fixed: facility and equipment, approval and licensing, distribution infrastructure, marketing
Costs – Variable: materials/production per drop, testing
Customers: age range, market share, adoption rates

questions.prompt: Estimate the total addressable US market (number of patients who would adopt Magic Eye Drops over the 20-year patent life).
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population (~300M) into age cohorts, apply a rate of sight problems per cohort, then apply a rate of adoption. Strong candidates explain WHY adoption rates differ (e.g., young children excluded because eyes are still developing; elderly have fewer benefit-years remaining). Bonus: recognize that at 3.5% annual growth the market doubles in ~20 years (Rule of 70), giving ~100M total consumers.

math.setup: Divide ~300M US population into 6 age bands of 50M each. Apply sight-problem rate and adoption rate per band.
steps: Growth adjustment: at 3.5%/yr the market doubles over 20 yrs (Rule of 70) → true market = ~100M consumers

questions.prompt: Estimate total revenue over the life of the patent.
questions.guidance: Candidate should choose a pricing strategy. Using competitive pricing, the benchmark is annual corrective-lens cost of ~$200. Eye drops are a one-time purchase replacing years of spending, so the value-based price could be higher; risk/novelty may justify a discount. Interviewer should accept reasonable adjustments. Discount rate = 0%, so no NPV discounting is needed.

math.setup: Market Size × Annual Value of Magic Eye Drops × Patent Life = Total Revenue

questions.prompt: Brainstorm cost drivers, then calculate total costs using the figures the interviewer provides.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify fixed costs (facility, marketing, distribution, overhead) and variable costs (production per drop, testing) before receiving numbers. After brainstorming, interviewer provides figures; candidate calculates.

math.setup: Sum operating costs over 20 years plus overhead (33% of operating costs).
steps: Production: $20/drop × 2 eyes × 50M patients = $2B (one-time treatment for base market)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key cost drivers for commercializing Magic Eye Drops?

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Raw materials and production cost per drop

categories.name: Other Considerations
ideas: Management and overhead (typically ~33% of operating costs)
Piracy and patent enforcement costs in international markets

recommendation: Dr. Rossman should ask approximately $392B for the rights to Magic Eye Drops ($400B revenue – $8B costs over the 20-year patent life).
Sales revenue could potentially continue even after patent expiration, which provides upside to this valuation.
risks: A substitute or improved product (e.g., better laser surgery or another breakthrough) may be invented during the patent period, eroding market share.
The exclusive patent will not fully prevent pirating in all countries, which could reduce addressable market in some geographies.
next_steps: Solicit buyers broadly and focus outreach on strategic acquirers (large pharma, medical device companies).
Attempt to start a competitive bidding war to maximize sale price.
Speak at industry conferences to generate awareness and inbound interest.
